title: SLA-driven batch sculpting lab notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working lab notebook for a set of micro-experiments that explore 'batch sculpting' — dynamic shaping of batch formation and admission to hit percentile SLOs rather than only optimizing for average throughput. The motivation is simple: some customers require tight p99/95 SLOs for interactive features and current continuous-batching heuristics trade away tail latency under realistic mixed workloads.

Goals:
- Produce a small, reproducible matrix of changes to the batching pipeline that can reduce 95/99p latency at modest throughput/cost impact.
- Identify the dominant system-level bottlenecks for the sculpted regimes (CPU scheduling, copies, kernel stalls, kv-cache misses).
- Propose a lightweight rollout plan (canary + rollback) for SLA-aware sculpting in Dedicated pools.

High-level idea: rather than a single timeout and one-size admission, use an SLA-driven controller that adapts three knobs per-queue: sculpt-window (ms), soft-cap (reqs/tokens), and deadline-confidence (multiplier on request age). Additionally add a probabilistic admission gate that preferentially favors older/high-SLA requests during microbursts.

Hypotheses (H):
H1: A modest sculpt-window (3–10ms) plus a soft-cap significantly reduces p99 latency for mixed small/large request mixes compared to static timeouts with <6% throughput loss.
H2: Token-aware soft-cap (tokens rather than requests) yields better fairness across long-context and short-context tenants.
H3: The majority of p99 regressions in sculpted modes come from KV-cache misses compounded with small-batch kernel overheads rather than scheduling overhead.

Experiment design:
- System under test: staging serving cluster (4 x A100 equiv), model: small-medium Llama-family variant used for internal prod (seq len 1024 typical for long requests).
- Baseline: current continuous-batcher v1.9 default: timeout=12ms, max_batch_tokens=4096, fifo per-slot.
- Treatments (matrix):
  * sculpt-window: [2ms, 5ms, 10ms]
  * soft-cap-mode: [count, token]
  * soft-cap-value: [8 reqs, 16 reqs] or [4k tokens, 8k tokens] depending on mode
  * deadline-confidence: [1.0, 1.5 (aggressive), 2.0 (very aggressive)]
  * admission-prob: [none, 0.2 biased, 0.5 biased] (probabilistic pref favoring older/H-SLA)
- Workload patterns: synthetic replay from production traces (peak midweek), plus a synthetic two-cohort mix: cohort A (short, 16–64 tokens, 70% of requests), cohort B (long, 2k–4k tokens, 30%). Also run pure-short and pure-long as controls.
- Duration: 20 minute steady windows per configuration; 3 repeats per point. Interleaved baseline runs every 6 configurations to guard against drift.

Metrics captured (per-second time series and histograms):
- p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end and scheduling-only)
- tokens/sec and requests/sec (throughput)
- GPU utilization (SM%, mem%), kernel latency breakdown (attn, softmax, matmul) from tracer
- CPU scheduling time (time in scheduler queues), memcpy host<->device time
- KV-cache hit rate and median/mode cache miss penalty (ms)
- Batch size distribution (requests and tokens)
- Cost proxy: GPU-token*sec (rough cost metric)

Profiling instrumentation:
- Enable tracer with callsites around enqueue, coalescer, prefill, kernel launch. Add a lightweight flame for memcpy/serialize/deserialize.
- Surface per-request tags: cohort, tenant-sla (low/med/high), request-size-buckets.

Preliminary results (summary from first 54 runs):
- Best single config for p99 reduction on mixed workload: sculpt-window=5ms + token-soft-cap=8k + deadline-confidence=1.5 + admission-prob=0.2
  * p99: baseline 314ms -> sculpted 198ms (37% reduction)
  * p95: baseline 112ms -> sculpted 94ms (16% reduction)
  * throughput: -4.8% requests/sec, -6.2% tokens/sec
  * GPU util: baseline 64% -> sculpted 60% (small loss)
  * KV-cache hit rate: unchanged (46%)
- Observed cost per token: +3.1% (due to lower GPU packing efficiency)
- Token-soft-cap consistently outperformed request-count soft-cap in mixed workloads: token-aware shaping prevented starving short requests when a few long requests were present.

Profiling notes (where time goes):
- Scheduling-only latency (time spent waiting in coalescer/slot allocation) dropped by ~40% in sculpted mode for short requests. Good: sculpting reduces queue wait for high-SLA items.
- Kernel level: small-batch penalty still visible — per-kernel launch overheads dominate for batches < 6 sequences. When sculpting reduces average batch depth, kernel inefficiency explains the throughput loss.
- Memcpy: increased variance in host->device memcpy during sculpted config, likely due to more frequent, smaller copies. Suggest exploration of batched memcpy pooling or pinned-buffer reuse.
- KV-cache: we saw no major change in aggregate hit rate, but long-request cohorts experienced slightly higher miss-tail (95th percentile miss penalty +14ms). Hypothesis: sculpting caused earlier eviction for long contexts as cache was reused for short bursts.

Interpretation and tradeoffs:
- Sculpting is effective at bringing down tail latency for mixed workloads with minimal throughput impact if token-awareness is used.
- The main cost is packing efficiency (kernel small-batch penalty) and copy overheads; KV-cache interactions are secondary but visible for long contexts.
- Recommendation: pair sculpting with a small batching micro-optimizer that consolidates memcpy and coalesces GPU-side IO for small-batch windows. That should recover most of the 3–6% throughput loss while keeping p99 gains.

Open questions and risky assumptions:
- We assume production duty cycle will see similar cohort mixes — need more trace stratification across tenants (some customers are extremely long-tail in length).
- Rollout safety: sculpting could increase jitter for low-SLA bulk workloads; need strong canary telemetry with per-tenant p95 tracking and automatic per-tenant disable.
- Does deadline-confidence multiplier interact poorly with autoscaling policies (e.g., aggressive deadline triggers causing unnecessary scale-ups)? Monitor scaling events during canary.

Next steps / action items:
- [Aisha] Build a minimal memcpy-pooling patch to reduce small-copy overheads (PR target: Q2 sprint). Linked: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1883 (WIP).
- [Marco] Add per-tenant p95/p99 telemetry to the canary dashboard and create an alert runbook (due 2025-06-25).
- [Hannah] Run longer-duration (4hr) stability passes on Dedicated pools with sculpting enabled at 0.2 admission bias; capture scaling events.
- [Omar] Prototype an on-device small-batch combiner that defers memcpy for short windows (experimental kernel scheduler).

Cheap experiments to validate next:
- Run token-aware sculpting + memcpy-pooling patch on pure-short workload to confirm throughput recovery.
- Simulate extremely skewed tenant distribution to test per-tenant disable logic.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Could use a tiny ML predictor (logistic regression) to predict whether a waiting request will soon be joined by another compatible request — informing timeout scaling per-slot. Keep it simple: features = recent interarrival, request-size, tenant-type.
- Consider shipping sculpting as a per-pool config flag with default off; turn on for Dedicated low-latency tiers first.
- Add a telemetry tag 'sculpting_active' to traces to simplify postmortem comparison.

Appendix: quick experiment matrix snapshot (first 12 runs):
- Run 1: baseline (timeout=12ms) -> mixed -> p99 314ms
- Run 2: sculpt 2ms, count-softcap 8reqs, dc=1.0, no admission -> p99 255ms
- Run 3: sculpt 5ms, token-softcap 8k, dc=1.5, adm=0.2 -> p99 198ms (best so far)
- Run 4: sculpt 10ms, token-softcap 4k, dc=2.0, adm=0.5 -> p99 220ms, throughput -9%
- Run 5: sculpt 5ms, count-softcap 16reqs -> p99 228ms
- Run 6: baseline repeat -> p99 312ms
- Run 7-12: repeated treatments (variance within ±4% p99 across repeats)

If you want to rerun any specific point, call out the run number and I can requeue in the staging harness.

-- Aisha
